Does the lowest-leg parlay work in the NBA?

Not as an edge. Across 154 finished games from Oct 20 to Nov 9, the lowest NBA line hit 7818 of 9989 (78.3%), priced at 75¢. The NFL rule (85¢+ with a tight book) picks legs that hit 90.2%, a bit below their 92¢ price, so those parlays hit less often than they're priced. Rebounds and assists hold their floors best, and points and threes only hold up for each team's top-2 scorers. Limited to those, a 6-leg parlay hit 80 of 107 games (75%, priced at 74%), and it still lost 5% after the spread. That rule was picked on these same 20 days, so the real number is likely worse.

Can a search find a better rule?

We tried 324 rule combinations: 5 stat sets, 3 role filters, 3 price floors, 3 to 7 legs and 2 team caps. Each was picked on the first 71 games (before Oct 30) and then scored on the 83 games after. A rule with a real edge should keep it on games it hasn't seen.

None held up. Only 8 of 324 rules made money over the whole season, about what luck alone gives. A rule's return on the first half barely predicted its return on the second (correlation 0.11). The 10 best first-half rules averaged -5.7% afterwards, against -7.9% for all rules.

Every lowest leg

How to read this

  • Every finished regular-season game from Oct 20 with Polymarket US player ladders. The "lowest leg" is the lowest rung of each player's ladder for each stat.
  • Results are the exchange's settlements. Actual stats and minutes are from ESPN box scores. Players who didn't play are VOID and left out.
  • Price is the midpoint of the last price snapshot before tip-off. Returns use the tip-off ask, before fees, and thin books may not fill at those prices.
  • Reasons under each leg use game logs from last season and this one, from NBA.com box scores (half-time-probs project), topped up with ESPN box scores for the latest days.
  • Unlike the NFL, nobody here is removed for leaving injured. NBA in-game exits are rarer and harder to spot, so those misses stay in.
